y-m-29-01.title: Which plan suits my younger sibling better?
y-m-29-01.topic: Using linear functions: comparing two plans and the usage at the boundary
y-m-29-01.goal: Express two quantities that grow at a constant rate, like charges, with linear functions, learn that which is cheaper can depend on the usage, revise your judgment and confidence each time new data arrives, and design a new plan that fits the conditions yourself.
y-m-29-01.material:
My younger sibling wants to choose a mobile phone data plan. If the monthly usage is x GB (a number 0 or more, decimals possible), the monthly charge y (원) of the two plans is as follows.
Plan A: basic fee 3000원 + 500원 per 1GB, that is, y=500x+3000
Plan B: basic fee 6000원 + 300원 per 1GB, that is, y=300x+6000
(y=500x+3000 is read as 'y equals five hundred x plus three thousand'. Assume the charge per 1GB does not change even if the usage is large. The amounts are made-up values.)
y-m-29-01.thinking.0: Postponing judgment when information is lacking
y-m-29-01.thinking.1: Revising the range and confidence of a judgment with new data
y-m-29-01.thinking.2: Interpreting the boundary where the better side changes
y-m-29-01.thinking.3: Making several designs that satisfy the conditions
y-m-29-01.prereq.0: The meaning of the linear function y=ax+b: it starts from the base value b and adds a each time x increases by 1 (middle school grade 2 level)
y-m-29-01.prereq.1: Calculating the value of an expression by putting numbers in for a variable
y-m-29-01.s.s1.prompt: Data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your thought about which plan is better.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put the usage given at each step into the two expressions y=500x+3000 and y=300x+6000 and calculate the charges directly.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write the two calculated charges side by side for each usage, and see whether which one is cheaper changes as the usage increases.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Right now only the expressions of the two plans are known. You do not yet know how much data your sibling uses in a month.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which plan can you say suits your sibling better?
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.after: A has a low basic fee and a high charge per 1GB, and B is the opposite. When it is crossed like this, the better side can differ when the usage is small and when it is large. Since you do not know the usage right now, it is hard to decide.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A, which has the cheaper basic fee, is cheaper in every case regardless of usage
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You only compared the basic fee. Calculate directly what the two charges are when the usage is very large.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: B, which has the cheaper charge per 1GB, is cheaper in every case regardless of usage
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You only compared the charge per 1GB. Calculate the two charges when the usage is close to 0GB.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It can differ depending on the usage, so I can decide only after knowing the usage
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a thought that noticed that the basic fee and the charge per 1GB are crossed. At what usage the better side changes becomes the next question.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: In the end the two charges become the same amount, so there is no difference whichever you choose
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even if there is a usage where they are equal, at other usages there is a difference. Calculate the two charges for several usages.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Your sibling's usage for the last 3 months was 8GB, 10GB, and 12GB. Calculating the charges, A is 7000원, 8000원, and 9000원, and B is 8400원, 9000원, and 9600원.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: If you choose a plan with this data, what do you think?
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.after: In the range 8 to 12GB, A stays cheaper. For this range, choosing A is based on calculation, and you only need to add the caveat that outside the range it must be checked separately. At this step there is no new information to change your mind.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A was cheaper in all three months, so A is better. But it can change if the usage changes
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You used the actual calculation results as evidence, and also thought about in what range the judgment holds.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: B, which has the cheaper charge per 1GB, is better. The unit price matters more than the three months of calculation results
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: In the actual calculations of all three months, A was cheaper. Check whether you set the calculation results aside by looking only at the unit price.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: I am sure that A is cheaper no matter how much the usage becomes in the future
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You did not calculate the case of using much more than 12GB. Compare the two charges at 30GB.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The usage of the three months is similar, so I cannot say anything about which is better
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: In the range 8 to 12GB, A stayed cheaper. If you state it with a range, you can make a judgment.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Your sibling says that from next month they will watch video lectures, so the usage will be between 18GB and 22GB.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now which plan do you think is better?
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A is still better. Because A came out cheaper for the past 3 months
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The usage in the past data was 12GB or less. Calculate the two charges directly at the new usage of 18GB.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You judged the whole new range at once, using the usage where they become equal as the standard. You reflected that the range where the past judgment held and the new range are different.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: B is better. At 18GB, B 11400원 < A 12000원, and at 22GB, B 12600원 < A 14000원
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You checked by calculating directly at both ends of the range. You revised your judgment to fit the new data.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The range 18 to 22GB is wide, so I cannot decide which is cheaper
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If the same side is cheaper at both ends (18GB, 22GB), you can check whether the same side is cheaper in between too. See whether the usage where they become equal is outside the range.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.reflect: How did your judgment change over the three steps? Which information changed your judgment, and which only increased your confidence without changing the judgment? Was the earlier judgment (A is better) 'wrong', or 'right only in that range'?
y-m-29-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose the usage at which the two charges become equal, and the fitting statement of what that value tells you.
y-m-29-01.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, put the given usage into the two expressions and write the charges of A and B side by side.
y-m-29-01.s.s2.hint.1: If a value where the charges are equal comes out, also calculate once which side is cheaper at a smaller usage and at a larger usage than that value.
y-m-29-01.s.s2.explain: From 500x+3000=300x+6000, 200x=3000, so x=15. At 15GB both charges are 10500원, and if you use less than 15GB, A is cheaper; if you use more, B is cheaper. A, with the low basic fee, is better at first, but since its charge per 1GB is higher, the gap shrinks as the usage grows and flips at 15GB.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.prompt: Design a new plan C for when your sibling uses 18GB to 22GB. The charge of C is y=(charge per 1GB)×x+(basic fee). Conditions: the basic fee is 2000원 or more (in units of 100원), and the charge per 1GB is 200원 or more (in units of 50원). When using 18GB and when using 22GB, it must be cheaper than both A and B, and when using 2GB, it must be more expensive than A (so that A is better for people who use little). Make two different plans.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write down what the cheaper charge between A and B is at 18GB and at 22GB.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.hint.1: Decide one basic fee, change the charge per 1GB, and check the three conditions of 18GB, 22GB, and 2GB one at a time.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.ok.c1: The basic fee and the charge per 1GB fit the given range and unit.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.fail.c1: Make the basic fee 2000원 or more in units of 100원, and the charge per 1GB 200원 or more in units of 50원.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.ok.c2: It is cheaper than both A and B at 18GB and 22GB.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.fail.c2: At 18GB or 22GB, C is not cheaper than A or B. First write the cheaper charge between A and B at that usage and compare.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.ok.c3: At 2GB, C is more expensive than A.
y-m-29-01.s.s3.fail.c3: When using 2GB, the charge of C is not more expensive than the charge of A (4000원).
y-m-29-01.s.s3.explain: For example, if C=300x+4000, it is 9400원 at 18GB (cheaper than A 12000원 and B 11400원), 10600원 at 22GB (cheaper than A 14000원 and B 12600원), and 4600원 at 2GB (A is 4000원). There are many plans that satisfy the conditions. If it is cheaper at both ends (18GB, 22GB), it is also cheaper than A and B at the usages in between.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.after: For 18 to 22 GB, B is cheaper. The earlier judgment that A is cheaper at 8 to 12 GB was not wrong; it was right only in that range. As new information came in, the range where the judgment applies changed.
y-m-29-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: B is better. If you find the usage where the two charges are equal, 18 to 22 GB are all on the other side of that value, which is different from the range where the earlier judgment held
y-m-29-01.s.s2.o.a: 15 GB: using less than this, A is cheaper; using more, B is cheaper
y-m-29-01.s.s2.r.a: You pointed out together the value where they are equal and the meaning that the cheaper side switches before and after it.
y-m-29-01.s.s2.o.b: 6 GB: using less than this, A is cheaper; using more, B is cheaper
y-m-29-01.s.s2.r.b: At 6 GB, A is 6000 won and B is 7800 won, which are different. Put the same usage into both expressions and check whether the charges really become equal.
y-m-29-01.s.s2.o.c: 10 GB: using less than this, A is cheaper; using more, B is cheaper
y-m-29-01.s.s2.r.c: At 10 GB, A is 8000 won and B is 9000 won. That is not the value where the charges are equal.
y-m-29-01.s.s2.o.d: 15 GB: using less than this, B is cheaper; using more, A is cheaper
y-m-29-01.s.s2.r.d: You found the value where they are equal, but which one is cheaper is reversed. Calculate both charges at a usage below this value (e.g., 8 GB) to check.

y-m-29-02.title: Is the line that grows faster always on top?
y-m-29-02.topic: Linear functions: the meaning of slope and comparing the positions of two graphs
y-m-29-02.goal: Tell apart that slope tells 'how fast it grows' while the value at x=0 tells 'where it starts', and make and explain an example in which the slope is larger but the value is smaller.
y-m-29-02.material: Jia said, 'In a linear function y=ax+b, the one with the larger slope a increases more when x increases by 1. So if you compare two linear functions, the one with the larger slope always has the larger y value, whatever x is.' (y=ax+b is read as 'y equals a x plus b'. x can be any number, and in the problem below you test only integer x.)
y-m-29-02.thinking.0: Telling apart comparing speed and comparing values
y-m-29-02.thinking.2: Making counterexamples that fit the conditions
y-m-29-02.thinking.3: Thinking about in what range it holds
y-m-29-02.prereq.0: In a linear function y=ax+b, a is the amount y increases when x increases by 1, and b is the value when x=0 (middle school grade 2 level)
y-m-29-02.prereq.1: Putting numbers in for x to calculate y
y-m-29-02.s.s1.prompt: Read Jia's explanation line by line and choose the one line that was skipped without a reason.
y-m-29-02.s.s1.hint.0: Mark whether each line talks about 'how much it increases' or 'the size of the value'.
y-m-29-02.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate and compare the values of the two expressions at x=0 and x=1, and think about whether the step from line 3 to line 4 is justified.
y-m-29-02.s.s1.line.0: y=3x+1 increases by 3 each time x increases by 1.
y-m-29-02.s.s1.line.1: y=x+7 increases by 1 each time x increases by 1.
y-m-29-02.s.s1.line.2: Therefore y=3x+1 increases faster than y=x+7.
y-m-29-02.s.s1.line.3: Since it increases faster, the value of y=3x+1 is greater than the value of y=x+7 whatever x is.
y-m-29-02.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is the skipped line. Lines 1 to 3 are right. 'Increases faster' compares how much it increases, that is, the slope. Line 4 changed that into 'the value is greater'. If the starting values of the two functions (the y values when x=0, which are 1 and 7) are different, then even when how much they increase is different, the sizes of the values are not decided right away.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.prompt: Make examples showing that Jia's statement is wrong, using two different pairs of linear functions. The slope of the first function y=a₁x+b₁ must be greater than the slope of the second function y=a₂x+b₂, and at some integer x=t the value of the first function must be less than the value of the second function. a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂, and t are all integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the values of the two functions at x=0. Can you make the one with the larger slope start from a lower value?
y-m-29-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose b₁ small for the one with the larger slope and b₂ large for the one with the smaller slope, then change t and calculate and compare the two values.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.var.a1: Slope a₁ of the first function
y-m-29-02.s.s2.var.b1: b₁ of the first function (the value when x=0)
y-m-29-02.s.s2.var.a2: Slope a₂ of the second function
y-m-29-02.s.s2.var.b2: b₂ of the second function (the value when x=0)
y-m-29-02.s.s2.var.t: The value of x to compare, t
y-m-29-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Make a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂, and t all integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The slope of the first function is greater.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The slope a₁ of the first function must be greater than the slope a₂ of the second function.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.ok.c3: At x=t, the value of the first function, which has the larger slope, is actually smaller. Jia's statement is broken.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.fail.c3: At x=t, the value of the first function is not less than the value of the second function. Calculate the two values separately and compare.
y-m-29-02.s.s2.explain: Even if the slope is large, if the value at x=0 (b₁) is small enough, then for a while at the beginning the one with the smaller slope is on top. 'Increases faster' and 'the value is greater' are different statements. Even for the same two functions the result changes if you change t, so for one pair of functions, just changing t does not make a different example.
y-m-29-02.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Jia how 'the slope is large' and 'the value is large' are different. Use the numbers of the example you just made.
y-m-29-02.s.s3.hint.0: You may write the expressions of the two functions you just made and the value of t as they are.
y-m-29-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write the two things separately, like 'The slope is this much larger, but at x=t the values are like this,' and then add the reason.
y-m-29-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear that I calculated and compared the two values in the example I gave?
y-m-29-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I tell apart in my own words that 'how much it increases' and 'the size of the value' are different statements?
y-m-29-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I even think about from when the one with the larger slope becomes greater (or does not become greater)?
y-m-29-02.s.s3.model.0: A large slope means y increases more when x increases by 1. Still, for y=3x+1 and y=x+7, at x=1 they are 4 and 8, so the one with the larger slope is smaller. If the starting values are different, the sizes of the values can be reversed.
y-m-29-02.s.s3.model.1: Jia, slope is how fast it goes up, and it is different from the size of the value. For y=2x and y=-x+9, at x=1 they are 2 and 8. The slope of 2 is larger, but the value is lower. x has to get larger for it to reverse.

y-m-29-03.title: Which way was the graph of (x-2)² moved?
y-m-29-03.topic: Graphs of quadratic functions: the direction of translation in y=a(x-p)²+q
y-m-29-03.goal: Check whether the direction of movement decided only by the shape of the expression matches the values in a table, judge the direction of movement based on matching the places where the values are equal, and apply that rule to a new expression.
y-m-29-03.material:
Haeun talked about which way the graph of y=(x-2)² is moved from the graph of y=x². 'In the expression, 2 is subtracted from x, so x decreased by 2. So it is the graph moved to the left by 2.' (y=(x-2)² is read as 'y equals open parenthesis x minus two close parenthesis squared'. Translation means the whole graph moves while keeping its shape. Left is the direction where x gets smaller, and right is the direction where x gets larger.) Haeun made a table by putting numbers in for x to find y. Read the table horizontally.
  x          | -2 | -1 |  0 |  1 |  2 |  3 |  4
  y=x²       |  4 |  1 |  0 |  1 |  4 |  9 | 16
  y=(x-2)²   | 16 |  9 |  4 |  1 |  0 |  1 |  4
y-m-29-03.thinking.0: Comparing the shape of the expression with the evidence of values
y-m-29-03.thinking.1: Building a general rule from the correspondence of several points
y-m-29-03.thinking.2: Verifying the rule by applying it to a new expression
y-m-29-03.prereq.0: The graph of the quadratic function y=x² (a parabola) and the smallest value 0 occurring at x=0 (middle school grade 3 level)
y-m-29-03.prereq.1: Calculating y by putting numbers into an expression
y-m-29-03.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the table, choose the most fitting way to judge Haeun's statement ('the graph moved to the left by 2').
y-m-29-03.s.s1.hint.0: Find at which x in the table the place where y=x² has its smallest value (0) appears for y=(x-2)².
y-m-29-03.s.s1.hint.1: Find the x where y=x² gives the same value (1 or 4), and compare it with the x where y=(x-2)² gives the same value.
y-m-29-03.s.s1.o.a: Haeun is right. In the expression x decreased by 2, so it moved to the side where x is smaller, that is, to the left by 2
y-m-29-03.s.s1.r.a: You decided the direction only from the shape of the expression (x-2). You did not check whether the values in the table match that direction.
y-m-29-03.s.s1.o.b: The values of y=(x-2)² are largest, 16, on the left (x=-2), so the graph leans to the left
y-m-29-03.s.s1.r.b: You only looked at the place where large values appeared in the table. Compare the place where the smallest value 0 appears with y=x².
y-m-29-03.s.s1.o.c: The x giving the values 0, 1, and 4 of y=x² are all 2 greater in y=(x-2)²
y-m-29-03.s.s1.r.c: You matched up whether several values are moved by the same rule. You used the movement of the whole graph, not one point, as evidence.
y-m-29-03.s.s1.o.d: A few points in the table cannot tell the direction of movement, so you cannot judge until you draw the graph
y-m-29-03.s.s1.r.d: This is a careful thought that it is hard to be sure from just a few points. But if several values in the table are moved by the same rule, evidence is accumulating. Try matching the places of the values 0, 1, and 4.
y-m-29-03.s.s1.explain: In y=x², the value 0 occurs at x=0, the value 1 at x=±1, and the value 4 at x=±2. In y=(x-2)², the value 0 occurs at x=2, the value 1 at x=1 and 3, and the value 4 at x=0 and 4. All are 2 to the right (the side where x gets larger). Haeun's direction does not match the table. This is because x has to be 2 larger to get the same y value.
y-m-29-03.s.s2.prompt: Use the rule you learned from the table on y=(x+3)²+1. What are the coordinates of the point where the value of y is smallest (the vertex) on this graph? (The +1 is added to the whole (x+3)².)
y-m-29-03.s.s2.hint.0: First find the value of x that makes x+3 equal to 0.
y-m-29-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the value of y=(x+3)²+1 directly at that x, and check whether it is smaller than that value at other x.
y-m-29-03.s.s2.r.a: Check directly whether the x that makes x+3 equal to 0 is 3. If you put in x=3, what is (x+3)²?
y-m-29-03.s.s2.r.b: You handled the number added to x and the number added to the whole expression separately.
y-m-29-03.s.s2.r.c: You decided the position of x correctly. But the expression has +1 at the end, so check whether y can be less than 0 where the value of y is smallest.
y-m-29-03.s.s2.r.d: Check the signs of both the x position and the y position again. Put x=3 and y=-1 into the expression.
y-m-29-03.s.s2.explain: (x+3)² has its smallest value 0 when x=-3, and adding 1 to that makes the smallest value 1. The vertex is (-3, 1), and this graph is y=x² moved 3 to the left and 1 up. The number added to x appears in the direction opposite to the sign seen in the expression, and the number added to the whole expression appears with its sign as it is, upward (+) or downward (-).
y-m-29-03.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Haeun which way y=(x-2)² is moved from y=x², and how she can check it using the table or values.
y-m-29-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write in one sentence where the place with the smallest value 0 in the table went from and to.
y-m-29-03.s.s3.hint.1: Apply that movement to other values (1 or 4) too, and sum up what was wrong in Haeun's statement.
y-m-29-03.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Haeun, if you look at the table, ...
y-m-29-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did the evidence I wrote come from the values in the table, not from the shape of the expression?
y-m-29-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I compare the places where y=x² and y=(x-2)² give the same value?
y-m-29-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I say not only the direction but also how much it moved?
y-m-29-03.s.s3.model.0: If you make a table, y=x² has its smallest value 0 at x=0, and y=(x-2)² becomes 0 at x=2. So it was moved to the right by 2.
y-m-29-03.s.s3.model.1: For x-2 to be 0, x has to be 2, so the vertex went from (0, 0) to (2, 0). If you put in values, the same y value appears where x is 2 larger. So it is the side where x gets larger, the right.

y-m-29-04.title: A vegetable garden against a wall: which shape has the largest area?
y-m-29-04.topic: Using quadratic functions: when a rectangle against a wall has the largest area
y-m-29-04.goal: Think about whether a rule that worked before (with the same perimeter, a square has the largest area) still works under new conditions, find several designs that satisfy the conditions, and explain why the area grows and then shrinks.
y-m-29-04.material: You want to make a rectangular vegetable garden against a wall using 20m of wire fence. No fence is needed on the side with the wall, and the fence goes around only the other three sides. You use all of the fence with none left. If the lengths of the two sides perpendicular to the wall are each x m and the length of the side parallel to the wall is y m, then 2x+y=20. The fence is cut in units of 1m, so x and y are natural numbers, and the area of the garden is x×y (m²).
y-m-29-04.thinking.0: Checking the conditions under which a rule works
y-m-29-04.thinking.1: Finding solutions that satisfy several conditions at once
y-m-29-04.thinking.2: Explaining why the product of two changing quantities grows and then shrinks
y-m-29-04.prereq.0: The area of a rectangle, multiplying natural numbers (elementary to middle school grade 1 level)
y-m-29-04.prereq.1: Finding values by putting numbers into an expression
y-m-29-04.s.s1.prompt: Minsu said, 'When the perimeter of the fence is fixed, a square had the largest area, so here too the area will be largest when x and y are equal.' What is the most fitting way to handle this statement?
y-m-29-04.s.s1.hint.0: If x=y, think about what x would be in the expression 2x+y=20 made from 20m of fence.
y-m-29-04.s.s1.hint.1: For x equal to 1, 2, 3, ..., find y and the area each time and write them side by side.
y-m-29-04.s.s1.o.a: He is right. Whatever shape the fence makes, the closer it is to a square, the larger the area always is, so there is no need to compare directly
y-m-29-04.s.s1.r.a: You used the rule as it is without checking in what situations it works. This time, because of the wall, the number of sides the fence goes around has changed.
y-m-29-04.s.s1.o.b: The number of sides with fence changed to three, so I will not use that rule and will instead change x and compare the areas
y-m-29-04.s.s1.r.b: You thought about whether the conditions under which the rule worked and the conditions this time are the same, and decided to compare values directly.
y-m-29-04.s.s1.o.c: He is wrong. For any fence, the thinner and longer you make it, the larger the area, so make x the smallest
y-m-29-04.s.s1.r.c: You completely reversed the earlier rule. Calculate the area of the thin, long shape (x=1).
y-m-29-04.s.s1.o.d: The length of the fence is the same, so the area is the same however you make it, and there is no need to change x and compare
y-m-29-04.s.s1.r.d: You thought that if the length is the same, the area is the same. Calculate the areas when x=1 and when x=5.
y-m-29-04.s.s1.explain: 'When the perimeter is fixed, a square has the largest area' is about the case where all four sides are enclosed with fence. This time the side along the wall needs no fence, so the fence goes around three sides. Besides, if x=y, then 3x=20, so x is not a natural number. Since the conditions changed, do not use the rule as it is; change x and find the areas directly.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.prompt: Using all 20m of fence, find three designs with different x in which the area of the garden is 42m² or more and the side y parallel to the wall is 8m or more. x and y are natural numbers.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.hint.0: First decide x, find what y becomes, and then calculate the area.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.hint.1: Make a table starting from x=1 in order, write y and the area side by side, and mark the rows that satisfy both conditions.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.var.x: Side perpendicular to the wall x (m)
y-m-29-04.s.s2.var.y: Side parallel to the wall y (m)
y-m-29-04.s.s2.ok.c1: x and y are natural numbers.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Make x and y natural numbers 1 or more.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.ok.c2: You used all 20m of fence with none left.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The fence length is not 20m. Calculate the sum of the three sides it goes around (2x+y).
y-m-29-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The area is less than 42m². Calculate the area x×y.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.ok.c4: The side parallel to the wall is 8m or more.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.fail.c4: The side y parallel to the wall is shorter than 8m.
y-m-29-04.s.s2.explain: The designs that satisfy the conditions are the four with x=3, 4, 5, 6 (areas 42, 48, 50, 48). For x=7 the area 42 is enough, but y=6 is shorter than 8, so it does not fit the conditions. For x=2, y=16, but the area 32 is not enough.
y-m-29-04.s.s3.prompt: If you make a table, the areas at x=4 and x=6 are both 48 and the area at x=5 is 50. Explain why the area is largest near x=5 and gets smaller toward both sides, by saying how y changes when x changes.
y-m-29-04.s.s3.hint.0: In the table, write line by line how much y decreases when x increases by 1 and how much the area increases or decreases.
y-m-29-04.s.s3.hint.1: Find the place where the amount the area increases keeps shrinking and then the area starts to decrease.
y-m-29-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say how each of the two numbers being multiplied, x and y, changes as x grows?
y-m-29-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason why there is a moment (x=5) when the area stops growing and starts shrinking?
y-m-29-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use the fact that the areas at x=4 and x=6 are the same in your explanation?
y-m-29-04.s.s3.model.0: When x increases by 1, y decreases by 2. When x is small, the effect of x growing is big, so the area grows, but after 5, the effect of y shrinking is bigger, so the area shrinks. So at x=5 it is the largest, 50.
y-m-29-04.s.s3.model.1: The area is x×(20-2x), and it is symmetric left and right around x=5. That is also why 4 and 6 are both 48. The farther x gets from 5, the smaller the area, so at 5 it is the largest, 50.

y-m-29-05.title: Can the water level record tell us what it will be in 10 minutes?
y-m-29-05.topic: Using linear functions: predicting from records and the range where the expression is valid
y-m-29-05.goal: Think about how far a linear function determined by two records is valid, decide what more to check before believing a prediction, and explain why the value of the expression and the value in the real situation can differ.
y-m-29-05.material: Water is being poured into an empty rectangular-box-shaped water tank with a hose. The moment the water starts being poured is 0 minutes, and the water level then (the height from the bottom to the water surface) is 0cm. The record says the water level was 12cm at 3 minutes and 20cm at 5 minutes. If the water flows in at the same speed all the time, the water level y (cm) at x minutes after the start is a linear function of x. Minjae said, 'It rises 4cm per minute, so the water level after 10 minutes is 40cm.' The height of the tank is not yet known.
y-m-29-05.thinking.0: Thinking about the range in which an expression applies
y-m-29-05.thinking.1: Sorting out information needed and not needed for a prediction
y-m-29-05.thinking.2: Stating a conclusion with conditions attached
y-m-29-05.prereq.0: Finding the slope of a linear function from two points: the change in y divided by the change in x (middle school grade 2 level)
y-m-29-05.prereq.1: Calculating values by putting numbers into an expression
y-m-29-05.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting judgment about Minjae's prediction 'the water level after 10 minutes is 40cm'?
y-m-29-05.s.s1.hint.0: From the records at 3 minutes and 5 minutes, find how many cm it rises per minute.
y-m-29-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write whether the value you calculate for the water level after 10 minutes at that speed is actually possible, and what is needed for it to be possible.
y-m-29-05.s.s1.o.a: If the water comes in steadily and the tank height is 40cm or more, it will be 40cm
y-m-29-05.s.s1.r.a: You judged with conditions attached how far the line determined by the records continues.
y-m-29-05.s.s1.o.b: There are only two records, so there is no way to guess the water level after 10 minutes
y-m-29-05.s.s1.r.b: If you assume the water flows in at a steady speed, the two records determine a line. If you accept the assumption, you can make a guess, and you must separately work out how far it is right.
y-m-29-05.s.s1.o.c: It was 12cm at 3 minutes and 20cm at 5 minutes, so after 10 minutes it will surely be 40cm
y-m-29-05.s.s1.r.c: You asserted 'surely'. Think about what conditions are needed for it to be 40cm.
y-m-29-05.s.s1.o.d: It was 20cm at 5 minutes and 5 more minutes pass, so it rises only 4cm more to 24cm
y-m-29-05.s.s1.r.d: Find again how much it rises in one minute. How many cm did it rise during the 2 minutes from 3 minutes to 5 minutes?
y-m-29-05.s.s1.explain: It rose 8cm during the 2 minutes from 3 minutes to 5 minutes, so it rises 4cm per minute. It was 0cm at the start, so y=4x. To say the level after 10 minutes is 40cm with this expression, two conditions are needed: (1) water keeps coming in at the same speed and (2) the height of the tank is 40cm or more. The two records determine the line, but how far that line is right is information outside the records.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose everything you need to check further to believe Minjae's prediction.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write in one sentence under what conditions the predicted 40cm could be a possible value.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what you should do to know whether the speed is the same between records too (at 4 minutes or 7 minutes).
y-m-29-05.s.s2.r.a: The color of the hose has nothing to do with how fast the level rises. Think about what affects the relationship between the water level and time.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.r.b: This is a thought that checks whether the predicted value is more than the height the tank can hold.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.o.c: The area of the bottom of the tank
y-m-29-05.s.s2.r.c: The speed at which the level rises is already given in the record in cm, so you do not need the area for predicting the water level.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.o.d: Measuring the water level at 7 minutes to see whether it matches the speed so far
y-m-29-05.s.s2.r.d: This is a thought that tests whether the same speed continues between records too.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.explain: For the prediction to be right, (1) the line (constant speed) must continue outside the records and (2) the height of the tank must be at least the predicted level. So the tank height and the water level at a time in between are needed. The color of the hose and the area of the bottom are not directly related to this prediction.
y-m-29-05.s.s2.acc.0: The tank height is the most important check. However, if you also do d, which checks whether the same speed really continues, you can trust the prediction more.
y-m-29-05.s.s3.prompt: You checked, and the water level at 7 minutes was 28cm and the height of the tank was 36cm. Using the expression y=4x, write what the water level is after 10 minutes and make clear whether it is fine to say 40cm. (Assume that when the tank is full, the water overflows or the hose is shut off.)
y-m-29-05.s.s3.hint.0: First find the value of x for which y is 36 in y=4x.
y-m-29-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the value of the expression and the actual water level can be the same at times after that x.
y-m-29-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find the time when y=4x gives 36cm and compare it with 40cm?
y-m-29-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that 'the expression is right but because of the tank height it can only be used up to this range'?
y-m-29-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you clearly write the water level after 10 minutes as a number?
y-m-29-05.s.s3.model.0: In y=4x, it reaches 36cm at 9 minutes. The tank height is 36cm, so it cannot rise any further at 10 minutes and it is 36cm (it is full and overflows), so you must not say 40cm.
y-m-29-05.s.s3.model.1: The expression is y=4x. If 4x=36, then x=9 minutes and the tank is full. At 10 minutes it is 36cm, not 40, and the water will overflow.

y-m-29-06.title: How does the width of a parabola change when a changes?
y-m-29-06.topic: The quadratic function y=ax²: how the sign and size of a affect the graph
y-m-29-06.goal: Judge step by step, based on the values in the tables, how the size and sign of a in y=ax² affect the width and the direction of opening, and find a counterexample and rewrite the rule.
y-m-29-06.material: Sua is comparing graphs (parabolas) of y=ax² such as y=x² and y=2x². (y=ax² is read as 'y equals a x squared'. a is a number other than 0.) The width of a parabola is described as the distance between the left point and the right point at the same height size (the absolute value of y). Sua thinks, 'The larger a is, the narrower the width will be.' Let's check whether this thought is right by looking at the tables one at a time.
y-m-29-06.thinking.0: Testing the first thought with new data
y-m-29-06.thinking.1: Finding a counterexample (testing even negative a)
y-m-29-06.thinking.2: Rewriting the rule together with its conditions
y-m-29-06.prereq.0: Making a table of values of the quadratic function y=x² and the shape of the graph (a parabola opening upward) (middle school grade 3 level)
y-m-29-06.prereq.1: The meaning of negative numbers and absolute value (middle school grade 1 level)
y-m-29-06.s.s1.prompt: Data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your thought about the width of the parabola.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.hint.0: In each table, compare the size of y (the value without its sign) for the same x.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.hint.1: Find, in the two expressions, the x that reaches the same height size (e.g. 2 or 12), and compare how far each is from the y-axis.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Table 1. When x is -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, y=x² is 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, and y=2x² is 8, 2, 0, 2, 8.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: For the same x, the value of y=2x² is greater than the value of y=x² (except x=0). How does the graph of y=2x² look compared with the graph of y=x²?
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.after: A larger value at the same x means it reaches the same height at a place closer to the y-axis (height 2: for y=x², x is about ±1.4, and for y=2x², it is ±1). So the width looks narrower. So far this does not contradict Sua's thought ('the larger a is, the narrower the width').
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The shape stays the same and the whole graph is moved upward
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: At x=0 both values are 0, so the lowest point is in the same place. It is not moved up; the way it rises is different.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It rises more steeply so the width looks narrower
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You used the fact that when the value at the same x is larger, it reaches the same height at a place closer to the y-axis.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It spreads out more widely so the width looks wider
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: When the value at the same x is larger, it reaches the same height sooner. Find the x that reaches height 2 in the two expressions and compare.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The shapes of the two graphs are exactly the same and only the values come out differently
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The y values differ at the same x, so it is hard to say they have the same shape. Compare the left-right distance at height 2.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: How is the width of y=(1/2)x² compared with y=x²? How can Sua's thought ('the larger a is, the narrower the width') be viewed with this data?
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.after: At the same x the value is smaller, so to reach the same height you have to go farther from the y-axis. So the width is wider. As a gets larger, 1/2, 1, 2, the width gets narrower, so Sua's thought is right up to here.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is narrower than y=x². Whenever a is not 1, the width is always narrower
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: At the same x the value is smaller. Check whether, to reach the same height, it gets closer to or farther from the y-axis.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The width is exactly the same and only the values got smaller, so it is the same shape
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The x that reaches the same height is different. Compare the x of the two expressions at height 2.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is wider than y=x². As a gets larger it gets narrower, so it matches Sua's thought
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You tested Sua's thought by putting the order of the sizes of a together with the order of the widths.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is wide only near x=0, and farther away it actually gets narrower
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: At other x in the table the value is also smaller in the same direction. Look at whether the whole thing has the same tendency, not just one place.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.info: Table 3. y=-3x² is -12, -3, 0, -3, -12 when x is -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and opens downward. y=(1/2)x² is 2, 0.5, 0, 0.5, 2 and opens upward. Compare the width as the distance between the left point and the right point at the same height size (|y|).
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which do you think has the narrower width, y=-3x² or y=(1/2)x²?
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.after: Looking at where the height size is 12, y=-3x² has x=±2 and y=(1/2)x² has x=±√24, about ±4.9. So y=-3x² is narrower. Sua's thought 'the larger a is, the narrower the width' is not right when a is negative. The width depends not on the sign of a but on the size of a (the value without its sign).
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: y=-3x² is narrower. The sign decides the direction, and the size of 3 without its sign decides the width
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You made the distinction that the sign is the direction and the size is the width.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: y=(1/2)x² is narrower. 1/2 is a larger number than -3, so Sua's thought is right
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You applied Sua's thought as it is. Find, in the two expressions, the x that reaches the same height size (e.g. 12).
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: One opens upward and one opens downward, so their widths cannot be compared
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: We decided to compare the width by the left-right distance at the same height size, regardless of the direction of opening. Compare again using that definition.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The widths of the two graphs are the same. The values -12 and 2 differ only in sign
y-m-29-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You compared the size of the numbers in the table including the sign. Find and compare the left-right distance at height size 12.
y-m-29-06.s.s1.reflect: What happened to Sua's thought ('the larger a is, the narrower the width') at each step? Which step's information made her fix that thought? Why was it too early to be sure before the third data, even though it looked right in the first two?
y-m-29-06.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the pairs that break Sua's thought 'the one with the larger a has the narrower width'. In each pair, if the one with the larger a does not have the narrower width (the same or wider), that pair breaks Sua's thought.
y-m-29-06.s.s2.hint.0: In each pair, first write which side has the larger a, and also write which side has the larger value without its sign (absolute value).
y-m-29-06.s.s2.hint.1: If the one with the larger a has the narrower width, the pair matches Sua's thought. Mark the pairs that do not.
y-m-29-06.s.s2.r.a: The one with the larger a (3) is actually narrower. This pair matches Sua's thought, so it is not a pair that breaks it.
y-m-29-06.s.s2.r.b: The widths of the one with the larger a (1/2) and the one with the smaller a (-1/2) are the same, so 'narrower' does not hold.
y-m-29-06.s.s2.r.c: The one with the larger a (4) is narrower, so this pair matches Sua's thought. It is not a pair that breaks it.
y-m-29-06.s.s2.r.d: The width of the one with the larger a (-2) is actually wider. You compared negative numbers.
y-m-29-06.s.s2.r.e: The width of the one with the larger a (1/2) is wider. You tested a pair with different signs.
y-m-29-06.s.s2.explain: A pair that breaks it is one where a is larger but the width is not narrower. b has equal widths, d has the wider one on the side with the larger a, and e also has the wider one on the side with the larger a. a and c are pairs that match Sua's thought. When looking for counterexamples, you need to check that you did not test only cases where a is positive.
y-m-29-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Sua's thought. Explain what about a decides the width of a parabola, giving one example.
y-m-29-06.s.s3.hint.0: You may use the numbers of one of the counterexample pairs you just chose as they are.
y-m-29-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence 'what value of a, when larger, makes the width how', and check it with the numbers of the example.
y-m-29-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. What decides the width is ...
y-m-29-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does my explanation include the case where a is negative?
y-m-29-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I keep to the point that the width is not 'the direction of opening' but 'the left-right distance at the same height'?
y-m-29-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: In the example I gave, did I check the order of the widths of the two graphs with values?
y-m-29-06.s.s3.model.0: What decides the width is not a itself but the absolute value of a. The larger the absolute value, the narrower it is. For example, a=-3 is a smaller number than a=1/2, but |-3|=3 is larger, so it is narrower.
y-m-29-06.s.s3.model.1: The sign only changes whether it opens upward or downward. For the width, drop the sign and look at the size of the number. y=-2x² and y=2x² have the same shape and differ only in the direction of opening. The larger the number, the narrower.

y-m-29-07.title: Making several parabolas that satisfy all the conditions
y-m-29-07.topic: The standard form of a quadratic function y=a(x-p)²+q: conditions given by the vertex and a point it passes through
y-m-29-07.goal: Translate several conditions into expressions accurately (checking for errors), make different quadratic functions that satisfy all the conditions yourself, and explain why in some cases there is no solution.
y-m-29-07.material: In the quadratic function y=a(x-p)²+q, the coordinates of the vertex are (p, q). (y=a(x-p)²+q is read as 'y equals a open parenthesis x minus p close parenthesis squared plus q'.) You want to find a quadratic function that satisfies all of the following conditions. 가) It is convex downward (a is positive). 나) The vertex is in the first quadrant (p>0, q>0). 다) The graph passes through the point (0, 7). a, p, and q are integers. First, let's check how Jihun turned the conditions into expressions.
y-m-29-07.thinking.0: Finding the error in a solution that turned conditions into expressions
y-m-29-07.thinking.2: Saying why there is no solution in some cases
y-m-29-07.prereq.0: In the quadratic function y=a(x-p)²+q, the vertex is (p, q) and the sign of a decides the shape (middle school grade 3 level)
y-m-29-07.prereq.1: Why a negative number squared is positive (sign rules)
y-m-29-07.s.s1.prompt: Jihun is turning conditions 가), 나), and 다) into expressions. He made a mistake on one line. Choose the line that is wrong first.
y-m-29-07.s.s1.line.0: It is convex downward, so a>0.
y-m-29-07.s.s1.line.1: The vertex (p, q) is in the first quadrant, so p>0 and q>0.
y-m-29-07.s.s1.line.2: It passes through the point (0, 7), so substituting x=0 and y=7 gives 7=a(0-p)²+q=-ap²+q.
y-m-29-07.s.s1.line.3: So we just need to find integers a, p, q that satisfy -ap²+q=7.
y-m-29-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the line that is wrong first. (0-p)² is (-p)², and (-p)×(-p)=p². Squaring removes the sign, so a(0-p)²=ap². So 7=ap²+q is right. Line 4 is also wrong because it continues the wrong expression of line 3 as it is. Lines 1 and 2 are right.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.prompt: Find three different quadratic functions y=a(x-p)²+q that satisfy all of: 가) convex downward (a is positive), 나) the vertex (p, q) is in the first quadrant (p>0, q>0), and 다) the graph passes through the point (0, 7). a, p, and q are integers.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.hint.0: Decide p, then find integers a and q, both positive, that satisfy the expression a×p×p+q=7.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change p to 1, 2, 3 and organize in a table whether there are possible (a, q).
y-m-29-07.s.s2.ok.c1: a, p, and q are integers.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Make a, p, and q integers.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.ok.c2: a is positive, so it is convex downward.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.fail.c2: To be convex downward, a must be positive.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The vertex (p, q) is in the first quadrant.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.fail.c3: For the vertex to be in the first quadrant, both p and q must be positive.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.ok.c4: The graph passes through the point (0, 7).
y-m-29-07.s.s2.fail.c4: When you put in x=0, y is not 7. Calculate a(0-p)²+q.
y-m-29-07.s.s2.explain: Putting in x=0 gives ap²+q=7. If p=1, then a+q=7, so (a, q) is one of six pairs: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1), and if p=2, then 4a+q=7, so only (1, 3). That makes seven in all. Different (a, p, q) are different functions.
y-m-29-07.s.s3.prompt: Expressions with p of 3 or more cannot satisfy all the conditions. Explain why, using the case p=3 as an example.
y-m-29-07.s.s3.hint.0: When p=3, write ap²+q=7 as 9a+q=7, put the smallest integer in for a, and find q.
y-m-29-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare what happens to p² and what effect it has on q as p grows to 4 and 5.
y-m-29-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write directly what the expression ap²+q=7 becomes when p=3?
y-m-29-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check the sign of q, using the case where a is the smallest value as an example?
y-m-29-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you even say what happens when p gets larger?

y-m-29-08.title: How many points does a line share with a parabola?
y-m-29-08.topic: Graphs of quadratic functions and lines: the number of intersection points and the value of k
y-m-29-08.goal: Test the idea 'it holds in a few examples, so it always holds' at the places where the value changes, make examples with 2 intersection points yourself, and explain with the smallest value why there is 1 intersection point or none.
y-m-29-08.material:
Draw the parabola y=x² and the line y=2x+k on the same coordinate plane. k is the number that decides the y-coordinate of the point where the line meets the y-axis. (y=2x+k is read as 'y equals two x plus k', and x²-2x is read as 'x squared minus two x'.) The x-coordinates of the intersection points of the two graphs are the x that satisfy x²=2x+k, that is, x²-2x=k. Below is a table of the values of x²-2x. Read the table horizontally.
  x       | -2 | -1 |  0 |  1 |  2 |  3 |  4
  x²-2x   |  8 |  3 |  0 | -1 |  0 |  3 |  8
y-m-29-08.thinking.0: Choosing where to test a generalization
y-m-29-08.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the conditions
y-m-29-08.thinking.2: Explaining why the number of intersection points changes
y-m-29-08.prereq.0: The graph of the quadratic function y=x² and a table of values of expressions such as x²-2x (middle school grade 3 level)
y-m-29-08.prereq.1: The x-coordinate of an intersection point is the x where the y values of the two expressions become equal
y-m-29-08.s.s1.prompt: In the table, when k=3 the x-coordinates of the intersection points are -1 and 3, and when k=0 they are 0 and 2, so there are 2 intersection points in both cases. Minjun thinks, 'Whatever number k is, the line y=2x+k meets the parabola at 2 points.' What is the best way to test Minjun's thought?
y-m-29-08.s.s1.explain: Piling up more examples of the same kind will not produce a counterexample. The number of intersection points can change near where the value of x²-2x is smallest (-1 when x=1 in the table). So choosing k near that value, such as k=-1 or k=-2, and checking is a real test. Let's explain the reason in the last step.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.prompt: Find three different values of k for which the line and the parabola meet at exactly 2 points and the x-coordinates of both intersection points are integers. Enter k and the x-coordinates x₁ and x₂ of the two intersection points. (x₁ and x₂ are integers from -9 to 9.)
y-m-29-08.s.s2.hint.0: In the table, find the rows where the same value appears twice, and write that value as k and the x values at that time as x₁ and x₂.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.hint.1: Put the k you found into x²=2x+k and calculate directly to check that both x are right.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.var.x1: The x-coordinate of one intersection point x₁
y-m-29-08.s.s2.var.x2: The x-coordinate of the other intersection point x₂
y-m-29-08.s.s2.ok.c1: k, x₁, and x₂ are integers that fit the conditions.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Make k, x₁, and x₂ integers and make x₁ and x₂ from -9 to 9.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The x-coordinates of the two intersection points are different from each other.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.fail.c2: If x₁ and x₂ are the same, there is one intersection point. Write two different values.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.fail.c3: x₁ or x₂ does not satisfy x²=2x+k. Substitute directly and compare both sides.
y-m-29-08.s.s2.explain: Find the rows in the table where the same value appears twice: the value 0 is at x=0 and 2, the value 3 is at x=-1 and 3, and the value 8 is at x=-2 and 4. Besides these, any integer pair with x₁+x₂=2 works (e.g. x=-3 and 5 gives k=15), and the two intersection points are the same distance left and right of x=1. Swapping x₁ and x₂ gives the same k, so it is the same example.
y-m-29-08.s.s3.prompt: When k=-1 there is only 1 intersection point, and when k=-2 there is none. Explain why, using the table (or the expression).
y-m-29-08.s.s3.hint.0: In the table, find the smallest of the values of x²-2x and at which x it occurs.
y-m-29-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether k=-1 and k=-2 are equal to or less than that smallest value, and think about whether there is an x that satisfies x²-2x=k then.
y-m-29-08.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. The values of x²-2x are ...
y-m-29-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give evidence for how much the smallest value of x²-2x is from the table (or the expression)?
y-m-29-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say where k=-1 and k=-2 each are compared with that value?
y-m-29-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use the connection that 'the x-coordinates of the intersection points are the x that satisfy x²-2x=k'?
y-m-29-08.s.s3.model.0: The smallest value of x²-2x is -1 when x=1. So if k=-1 they meet only at x=1, which is one point, and k=-2 is smaller than that, so there is no point where they meet.
y-m-29-08.s.s3.model.1: In the table, x²-2x never goes below -1. If k=-1, only x=1 works, and for k=-2 no x works, so there is no meeting point.
y-m-29-08.s.s1.hint.0: Read the values of x²-2x in the table from left to right and observe how the values change (keep growing, or change direction).
y-m-29-08.s.s1.hint.1: Pick a few values of k, count how many x in the table satisfy x²-2x=k, and compare roughly where k is when the count changes.
y-m-29-08.s.s1.o.a: Pick and test a few small natural numbers not in the table, such as k=1, k=2, k=5
y-m-29-08.s.s1.r.a: Testing is good, but there is no standard for what to look at when choosing values. First find where the values change in the table.
y-m-29-08.s.s1.o.b: Pick and test k near where the values in the table go down and then come back up (-1 or -2)
y-m-29-08.s.s1.r.b: You took as a clue that the place with the smallest value in the table is where the number of intersection points can change.
y-m-29-08.s.s1.o.c: Both examples were 2, so that is enough, and accept Minjun's idea as it is
y-m-29-08.s.s1.r.c: You asserted 'for any number' from few examples. There may be kinds of k that have not been tested yet.
y-m-29-08.s.s1.o.d: Test a few more values of k bigger than the table, such as k=8, k=15, k=24
y-m-29-08.s.s1.r.d: You are only piling up more of the same kind of value (large k). Look at how the values of x²-2x change in the table.
y-m-29-08.s.s3.model.2: x²-2x=(x-1)²-1, so it can't be less than -1. So k=-1 meets at only one place, x=1, and k=-2 has no solution.
